newsitem.title: RWANDA: Zaire refugee force now victim of numbers game.
newsitem.headline: Zaire refugee force now victim of numbers game.

text.p: A numbers game about Hutu refugees still stranded in eastern Zaire plunged planning for a multinational force into even greater confusion on Tuesday.
The United States, reluctant volunteers for the U.N.-backed force from the outset, radically scaled down its contribution after 500,000 of the refugees returned to Rwanda in five days.
Rwanda said no force was needed at all but Britain, France and the United Nations said about 700,000 refugees remained to be helped.
The human tide of refugees entering Rwanda from Goma, Zaire, since last Friday was down to a trickle on Tuesday.
But for many Hutus the suffering continued in the homeland they fled in 1994 after their kinsmen committed genocide against minority Tutsis and pro-opposition Hutus.
Tens of thousands of returning refugees demanding food on Tuesday blocked the streets of Nkamira, 21 km (13 miles) northeast of Gisenyi at the border with Zaire.
Defence Secretary William Perry said in Washington the U.S. still planned to join the Canadian-led force in its mission to help the refugees and encourage voluntary repatriation.
But he said the mass return justified a smaller force.
"Our current thinking is that U.S. contribution to this effort will be less than 1,000 troops. And these will be support logistics troops rather than combat troops," he said.
Rwandan Foreign Minister Anastase Gasana said in a statement that there were "hardly any" Rwandan refugees left in Zaire.
"These refugees who have returned home number 500,000 people, which broadly matches the real number of Rwandan refugees previously in eastern Zaire, in North and South Kivu," Gasana said.
His figures are contradicted by the official ones from the U.N. refugee agency, UNHCR, used by the world community.
UNHCR says there were 1.1 million Rwandan Hutus and 150,000 Burundian Hutus in camps in eastern Zaire before rebels took control of the area last month.

United Nations special envoy Raymond Chretien said in Kigali: "We have to know what is happening on the other side (of the border in Zaire). There are still approximately between 300,000-500,000 according to our best estimates and we have to know a bit more about what is happening to them."
The French foreign ministry said there were still 300,000 refugees in Bukavu, 200,000 near Goma and 200,000 in Uvira.

French President Jacques Chirac, speaking in Tokyo, backed the force despite the mass migration. He said one French objective was security in eastern Zaire -- a new mission for the force given a narrow mandate by the Security Council.
Britain also refused to bury the force, dogged by delays and confusion for the past fortnight, before it is even deployed.

"It is premature for the international community to conclude that there's nothing to be done because there are hundreds of thousands of refugees unaccounted for," Defence Minister Michael Portillo told the London Times.
A planning meeting in Stuttgart, Germany, on Thursday by governments who have pledged troops for the 10,000-strong force was partly pre-empted by Perry's announcement.
"This force will require considerably fewer troops than originally envisioned and will operate chiefly in Rwanda," he said.
Rwanda wants the resources originally set aside for the force to be diverted to resettle the returnees instead.
The peace force's future also appeared complicated by President Nelson Mandela, who said South Africa would contribute troops only if they were led by an officer from the region.
"I am not prepared to put my troops under any other commander except a commander from the Great Lakes," Mandela told reporters.
Two soldiers stood on guard outside the U.N. transit centre at Nkamira, stopping refugees from entering to have a rest, sleep and receive food as planned by the UNHCR.
The Rwandan authorities insist the refugees, exhausted by days of marching and sleeping rough, keep trudging onwards to their home villages.
The Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994 after mainly Tutsi rebels overran the country following the genocide of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus by Hutu extremists.
The few who have made it back to their villages said there had been no animosity from their former Tutsi neighbours.
Phinias Musemakweli, 43, returned to his home in a poor district in the outskirts of Ruhengeri with his wife and three daughters on Sunday.
"All the people welcomed us. We're happy because we have returned home at last. We have no fear for our security, the reason why we left Zaire was we were too frightened," he said.
His eldest daughter was asked whether Tutsis in the same district had said anything to them. "They saw us but have said nothing to us since we arrived," she replied.
"They are our brothers and welcomed us back," her father added quickly.
